key: D major in the orchestral original; band version transposed
intro: The United States Marine Band plays Elgar’s Pomp and Circumstance March No. 1 in D, Op. 39, in an arrangement for concert band. The march sets a long, singing tune between quick, sharp-edged sections, and in this arrangement woodwind and brass play both.

cues.title: Opening, Allegro, con molto fuoco
cues.text: Elgar marked the march Allegro, con molto fuoco (fast, with much fire). The opening phrases begin off the beat and continue in short bursts. In this recording the United States Marine Band plays the orchestral music on woodwind and brass.
cues.evidence: Elgar’s orchestral score, opening Allegro con molto fuoco: https://imslp.org/wiki/Pomp_and_Circumstance_March_No.1,_Op.39_No.1_(Elgar,_Edward). The Marine Band performance is identified by its Commons source; the arranger is unidentified.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Trio melody
cues.text: The trio has the melody later sung as Land of Hope and Glory. Its phrases rise, hold long notes and are followed by falling steps. Beneath it the accompaniment keeps a steady two-beat pulse.
cues.evidence: Boosey orchestral score, rehearsal I, Trio: melody and accompaniment. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/6/6e/IMSLP24159-PMLP23738-Elgar_-_Pomp_and_Circumstance%2C_Op._39%2C_No._1.pdf. The cue describes the tune at the established trio boundary in this band arrangement.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Honorary doctorate, Yale, 1905
cues.text: At Yale on 28 June 1905 Elgar received an honorary doctorate and wore the university’s blue robes. The orchestra played this march as the guests left. Other universities adopted it, and the tune became part of American graduation ceremonies.
cues.evidence: The Elgar Society, Why Americans graduate to Elgar: the degree ceremony, blue robes, recessional and later adoption. https://www.elgar.org/3pomp-b.htm

cues.title: Return of the quick march
cues.text: The march returns with its short, accented phrases and runs of quick notes. The long melody is absent for the whole section, and the bass and tune resume their brisk exchange.
cues.evidence: Boosey orchestral score, rehearsal M: return of the quick march. This arrangement’s established returning-march boundary is 3:20; the note concerns the shared themes.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Benson’s words, 1902
cues.text: In 1902 A. C. Benson wrote words to the trio melody for Elgar’s Coronation Ode, then revised them for the separate song Land of Hope and Glory. Clara Butt sang the solo version. Benson’s text includes an appeal for wider boundaries for the British Empire.
cues.evidence: The Elgar Society describes Benson’s versions, Clara Butt’s performance and reproduces the texts, including the appeal for wider imperial boundaries. https://www.elgar.org/3pomp.htm

cues.title: Coda
cues.text: After the broad tune ends, the march returns for a few quick phrases, marked a tempo and Più mosso from rehearsal T to the end. Short notes run through the closing passage. A sharp accent comes before the final held chord.
cues.evidence: Boosey orchestral score, rehearsal T to the end: a tempo and Più mosso. The band recording’s established coda boundary is 5:30; no particular instrumental allocation is asserted.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

fields.note: Rule 1, recording-specific US-law basis under 17 USC §105, not worldwide CC clearance. Commons separates Performance/Recording from Composition and attributes the file to a Marine Band official-duty recording with an official .mil source. No CC-NC licence appears in the Commons record or the reviewed official source wording. Marine Band boilerplate says its institutionally distributed recordings ‘may not be distributed for private use and are not for sale’ because appropriated funds are used: this is the agency’s physical-distribution policy, not a non-commercial copyright licence on the government performance. Official web downloads are offered separately. Direct upstream retrieval returned HTTP 403 during this research; the official page’s indexed distribution wording and reader-accessible download instructions were examined, and the file’s recording-specific Commons declaration remains explicit. No claim of worldwide rights or a cleared private arrangement is made.

composer.epithet: Composer of the Enigma Variations, a set of variations drawn from his friendships, who also recorded his own music for the gramophone.
facts: His father’s Worcester music shop; violin and organ; composition largely self-taught
Powick bandmaster, instrumental teacher and organist at St George’s, Worcester
Two symphonies; violin and cello concertos; Gerontius; five Pomp and Circumstance marches
Master of the King’s Musick from 1924; recordings of his own orchestral works
composer.background:
Elgar grew up among the instruments and sheet music in his father’s Worcester shop. William tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church; Edward studied the scores, learned several instruments and earned money with his violin. Born at Lower Broadheath on 2 June 1857, he had hoped to study at Leipzig, but the family could not afford it. Playing in the Three Choirs Festival orchestra, he learned the choral music of Handel and Mendelssohn as a member of the string section.

From 1879 to 1884 he was bandmaster at Worcester County Asylum, Powick. He trained members of staff to play for the patients and supplied quadrilles and polkas for the Friday-evening dances. He knew each player in this orchestra individually and had to write within their capabilities. He also taught in local schools and gave private lessons in Malvern. In 1885 he succeeded William at the organ of St George’s.
